slides.title: Sector Exposure & Executive Risk Outlook
slides.decision: Treat manufacturing cyber risk as an IT-dependent production, supplier-liquidity and product-liability issue.
slides.executive_conclusion: Exposure runs through the enterprise systems that release production and reaches the financial system through lost output, supplier liquidity and state-backed lending.
slides.visual_type: Judgement table with confidence and change conditions

elements.visible_text: Manufacturing cyber exposure in the period ran through the enterprise systems that release production, not through plant control systems; it reaches the financial system mainly through lost output, supplier liquidity and state-backed lending.

Evidence base: public records for the 13-month reporting period across the EU, EEA and UK with global comparison - company and securities filings, a national CERT alert, statistics-office and central-bank publications, an independent loss model, and ENISA, Dragos and Black Kite benchmarks.

Footprint: EU manufacturing employs 30.2 million people and produces 23.1% of business-economy value added. It drew 25.2% of EU ransomware claims in ENISA's latest review and about 65% of industrial ransomware in the latest quarter tracked by Dragos.
Production loss runs through IT dependency and precautionary shutdown, not direct operational technology (OT) compromise Medium Disclosed control-system manipulation causing damage at a manufacturer

elements.visible_text: Treat large manufacturing counterparties as IT-dependent production systems: ask how long they can release production without enterprise resource planning (ERP), manufacturing execution (MES) and identity services, and which suppliers depend on them for most of their revenue.

Quantified outcomes come from listed companies; supplier failures, ransom payments and the state of plant control systems are not publicly disclosed, so their absence is a disclosure gap, not evidence of zero effect.

slides.title: Key Threats & Top 5 Cyber Attacks
slides.decision: Weight reviews towards IT-OT production dependency, administrative tools and installed products.
slides.executive_conclusion: Five incidents meet the evidence standard; four stopped production through IT-side compromise and one compromised manufacturers' fielded controllers.
slides.visual_type: Named incident table with pattern list

elements.visible_text: Five incidents meet the evidence standard; four stopped production through IT-side compromise and one compromised manufacturers' controllers in customer premises, so both the enterprise estate and the installed product base are exposure points.

Threat pathways (patterns, not attacks): P1 ransomware and data extortion against enterprise IT; P2 destructive misuse of administrative platforms; P3 internet-exposed OT and fielded products; P4 supplier and service-provider compromise; P5 data theft with intellectual-property and export-control exposure.

ENISA found manufacturing the largest EU ransomware target, with exfiltration overtaking encryption; Dragos found no recent ransomware case reaching control-system manipulation, and 117 incidents at integrators and equipment makers in one quarter.

slides.title: Financial Impact: Manufacturing
slides.decision: Monitor counterparty liquidity and supplier concentration after a major manufacturer incident.
slides.executive_conclusion: Lost output and cash, not response cost, drive the financial effect; one OEM stop coincided with an officially recorded fall in vehicle output and needed state-backed lending.

elements.visible_text: Public financial evidence is thin and cannot be added up, but it consistently shows that lost output and cash, not response cost, drive the effect, and that a single OEM stop can show up in official vehicle-output statistics and require state-backed lending.
Evidence base: quarterly and annual company results, securities filings, the UK statistics office and central bank, an industry output series and the Cyber Monitoring Centre model of the JLR event.

JLR's labelled cyber costs were GBP 260 million over two quarters while quarterly free cash outflow reached GBP 1.5 billion. Transmission ran through a GBP 2 billion bridge facility, supplier prepayment via a banking partner and a government-guaranteed GBP 1.5 billion loan.

slides.title: Financial Impact: Worst-Case Scenarios
slides.decision: Identify shared platforms, vendors and supplier dependencies across manufacturing counterparties.
slides.executive_conclusion: Three distinct stress pathways converge on lost output, supplier liquidity and liability; they are not forecasts.

elements.visible_text: Three distinct stress pathways - a shared enterprise platform failure, a targeted stop at one large manufacturer and a compromise spreading through a supplier layer - converge on lost output, supplier liquidity and liability; they are stress narratives, not forecasts or loss estimates.

Evidence base: the JLR and medical-device shutdowns, a reported administrative-tool wipe, a cross-sector software outage, the controller compromise and a supplier hit through its IT provider; durations are illustrative.
Scenario 1 is broad and shallow, scenario 2 narrow and deep, scenario 3 broad through one supplier; all three reach banks through counterparty liquidity and liability rather than direct loss.
Ask which counterparties share the same enterprise platforms and OT vendors, and how many weeks of stop the largest manufacturing counterparties and their dependent suppliers can finance.
No probabilities are assigned because no defensible external basis exists; no multi-day common-platform outage across many manufacturers was observed in the period.

slides.title: Case Study: Jaguar Land Rover Cyber Incident
slides.decision: Treat a multi-week OEM stop as a foreseeable credit event for its supplier base.
slides.executive_conclusion: An enterprise-systems shutdown stopped production for about five weeks and transmitted to suppliers, bank liquidity, state guarantees and official vehicle-output statistics.

elements.visible_text: A precautionary shutdown of JLR's enterprise systems stopped production for about five weeks; in the following quarter wholesales fell 43% and free cash outflow reached GBP 1.5 billion, with tariffs and model wind-down also contributing. Suppliers needed customer-funded prepayment and the state guaranteed a GBP 1.5 billion bank loan.

Evidence base: company statements and four quarterly releases, the government guarantee release, a parliamentary letter, the statistics office, the central bank, an industry output series and the Cyber Monitoring Centre model; selected as the only in-period case with this depth.

Mechanism: production stopped because the systems that schedule, supply and release it were shut down; the plant control state and the initial access route were not disclosed, and a criminal group's claim was not confirmed.
Shutdown Day 0 Enterprise systems shut down; production and retail disrupted
row_cells: Enterprise systems shut down; production and retail disrupted

elements.visible_text: Liquidity Weeks 3-4 GBP 2 billion bridge facility; state guarantee announced to support the supply chain
row_cells: GBP 2 billion bridge facility; state guarantee announced to support the supply chain

elements.visible_text: Restart Week 6 Phased restart from engines and batteries; suppliers prepaid through a bank
row_cells: Phased restart from engines and batteries; suppliers prepaid through a bank

elements.visible_text: Normal production About week 11 Output back to normal; distribution still catching up
row_cells: Output back to normal; distribution still catching up

row_cells: GBP 260 million cyber costs; wholesales down 43.3%; vehicle-output fall recorded

Treat a multi-week stop at a large OEM as a foreseeable credit event for its supplier base: map supplier revenue concentration and know which supply-chain finance and guarantee channels would be used.
The case does not show the access route, plant control state, any ransom, the full-year cyber cost or any supplier insolvency; the economy-wide loss is modelled and covers UK operations only.

slides.title: Systemic Dependencies & Regulatory Outlook
slides.decision: Align counterparty documentation with product-security, liability and supplier obligations.
slides.executive_conclusion: Concentration sits in enterprise systems, administrative tools, OT vendors' installed bases, integrators and supplier tiers; regulation reaches most manufacturers through product law and contracts.
slides.visual_type: Dependency chain list and regulatory status table

elements.visible_text: Manufacturing concentration sits in enterprise systems, administrative tools, OT vendors' installed bases, integrators and just-in-time supplier tiers; regulation reaches most manufacturers through product law and contracts, with NIS2 limited to named activities.

Evidenced dependency chains: enterprise IT to production release; administrative tools to every device; OT vendor installed base to many customer sites; integrators and managed IT to several plants; one OEM to thousands of suppliers; manufacturer software to customers in other sectors.
Where NIS2 applies the population is large: Germany registered 4,739 entities under manufacturing of goods, while four Member States were referred to the Court of Justice for not transposing.

NIS2 Binding via national law Named activities: electronics, electrical equipment, machinery and vehicles (NACE C26-C30), medical devices, chemicals, food and pharmaceuticals; others only by national extension

National NIS2 extensions were not surveyed exhaustively; several legal texts were confirmed from official metadata and reproductions; market shares of manufacturing software and OT vendors are not public.

slides.title: Mitigation Strategies & Security Framework
slides.decision: Assign 1LoD owners and completion evidence to seven evidence-linked priorities.
slides.executive_conclusion: Seven priorities address the evidenced pathways, each with a challenge question, completion evidence and external trigger.
slides.visual_type: Action table with completion evidence and triggers

elements.visible_text: Seven evidence-linked priorities address the pathways: production release without IT, control of administrative tools, supplier liquidity, installed-base exposure, provider access, product-law readiness and insurance alignment.
A1 IT-OT production dependency (0-6 months) Can top counterparties release production and ship without ERP, MES and identity? Manual-release procedure; recovery tests Production-pause notice
row_cells: Can top counterparties release production and ship without ERP, MES and identity?

elements.visible_text: A2 Administrative tools (0-3 months) Do assessments test approval controls on mass wipe actions? Assessment evidence Alert on administrative-tool misuse
row_cells: Do assessments test approval controls on mass wipe actions?

elements.visible_text: A3 Supplier liquidity (0-6 months) Which programme suppliers depend on one customer? Concentration map; stress test OEM incident notice
row_cells: Which programme suppliers depend on one customer?

elements.visible_text: A4 Installed base (3-12 months) Do equipment makers track exposed and end-of-life units? Exposure and support register CERT alert naming a product
row_cells: Do equipment makers track exposed and end-of-life units?

elements.visible_text: A5 Provider access (3-12 months) Is provider remote access to OT restricted and logged? Access inventory and logs Disclosure citing an IT provider
row_cells: Is provider remote access to OT restricted and logged?

elements.visible_text: A6 Product-law readiness (0-6 months) Can counterparties meet new reporting and liability duties? Reporting procedure; support periods First enforcement action
row_cells: Can counterparties meet new reporting and liability duties?

elements.visible_text: A7 Insurance and contracts (6-12 months) Is customer-side disruption insured or priced? Documentation review Insurer product change
row_cells: Is customer-side disruption insured or priced?

elements.visible_text: Evidence base: CERT recommendations for exposed controllers, a US alert on administrative tools, the JLR supplier scheme, the independent loss model and the new product rules.
Frameworks are reference vocabularies, not law: NIST CSF 2.0 and its draft manufacturing profile, NIST SP 800-82, IEC 62443, ISO/IEC 27001 and 27036, and VDA ISA with TISAX for automotive.
Give each priority a First Line of Defence (1LoD) owner and a dated completion artefact, and escalate to the Risk Committee when a monitoring trigger fires.
Actions are sector priorities drawn from public evidence, not findings about any institution's controls, losses or risk appetite.
